title: Given candidates that may contain duplicates and a target, return all unique combinations summing to target, where each candidate may be used at most once.
shortTitle: Combination Sum II: each number used once, skip duplicates
keyPoints: Sort the candidates so duplicates are adjacent and pruning by overshoot is possible.
Recurse with i+1 (not i) so each candidate is used at most once.
Skip same-level duplicates: if i > start and cand[i] == cand[i-1], continue.
Record the path when the remaining target is zero; prune when cand[i] exceeds the remaining target.
The use-once rule plus the duplicate skip together handle collection from a multiset cleanly.
The same template works for Combination Sum (use i instead of i+1) and Subsets II (always record).

s1_definition.oneliner: Advance index by one (use-once) and skip same-level duplicates to get unique combinations from a multiset.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Combination Sum II** – find all unique combinations from a candidate array (with possible duplicates) that sum to a target, using each candidate at most once.
- **Sort first** – enables duplicate skipping and early pruning.
- **Use-once** – recurse with `i + 1` instead of `i`, ensuring each element is consumed only once.
- **Duplicate skip** – `if (i > start && cand[i] == cand[i-1]) continue` prevents duplicate combinations.
- **Prune** – break when `cand[i] > remaining` because the array is sorted.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India issues one-time cashback coupons, some of identical value, and a customer can use each coupon only once. To list every distinct set of coupons that reaches a target redemption amount, you consume each coupon at most once and avoid listing the same-valued coupon twice at the same choice point.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Candidates: [100, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500] (sorted)
  Target: 600

  Backtracking tree (partial):
  ┌─ start=0, remain=600
  │
  ├─ choose 100 (i=0), remain=500, recurse start=1
  │   ├─ choose 100 (i=1), remain=400, recurse start=2
  │   │   ├─ choose 200, remain=200 --> choose ...
  │   │   ├─ choose 300, remain=100 --> no match
  │   │   └─ choose 400, remain=0 --> RECORD [100,100,400]
  │   ├─ choose 200 (i=2), remain=300
  │   │   └─ choose 300, remain=0 --> RECORD [100,200,300]
  │   └─ choose 500 (i=5), remain=0 --> RECORD [100,500]
  │
  ├─ choose 100 (i=1) SKIP: i>start && cand[1]==cand[0]
  │
  ├─ choose 200 (i=2), remain=400
  │   └─ choose 400, remain=0 --> RECORD [200,400]
  │
  └─ choose 300 (i=3), remain=300
      └─ choose 400, remain=-100 --> prune
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Combination Sum II differs from the first version in two ways: each candidate may be used at most once, and the input can contain duplicates that must not produce duplicate combinations. I sort the candidates so equal values are adjacent, and in the recursion I advance the start index by one after choosing an element, which enforces the use-once rule. To suppress duplicate combinations I skip any element whose index is beyond the current level's start and that equals the previous element.

The remaining-target logic is unchanged: I record when it reaches zero, abandon the branch when it goes negative, and because the array is sorted I break out of the loop as soon as a candidate exceeds the remaining target, pruning aggressively.

The three related problems, Combination Sum, Combination Sum II, and Subsets II, all share the same backtracking skeleton with the same-level-duplicate skip guard. The only differences are whether I recurse with `i` or `i + 1` and when I record the path. Recognising this shared template is the senior insight.

In my project at National Bank of India, a customer's wallet held one-time cashback coupons, some with identical values, and the system needed every distinct set of coupons that redeemed to an exact target. This use-once-plus-skip-duplicate template produced each valid set exactly once.

Remember one sentence: sort, recurse with i+1 for use-once, skip same-level duplicates with `i > start && cand[i] == cand[i-1]`, and break when the candidate exceeds the remaining target.
